human_tolerance.notes: Tolerant of human proximity and thriving in crowded urban and suburban neighbourhoods; uses buildings for food and nesting, 'as happy nesting in an attic as they are in a hollow tree'.

phases.name: mating
phases.note: Judgement window around 'Female fox squirrels come into estrus in mid-December or early January, then again in June'.

phases.name: young
phases.note: Judgement window for the first litter: gestation is 44-45 days from the December estrus, so 'the earliest litters appear in late January', and 'most births occur in mid-March'.

phases.name: young
phases.note: Judgement window for the second litter, from the June estrus and a 44-45 day gestation.

phases.name: caching
phases.note: Judgement window: 'Fox squirrels will form caches by burying food items for later consumption ... like to store foods that are shelled and high in fat, such as acorns and nuts', and autumn is when mast is available.

vocalizations.description: A series of barks, the most common vocalization of the species; a squirrel that barks is not usually the one giving a single alarm note but a whole series of them from an exposed perch.
Tooth chattering and breathy barks, given as an indication of stress.
Grunts and squeals, given by restrained animals and during male-male chases.

taxonomy.note: Linnaeus 1758, Sciurus niger; family Sciuridae per the GBIF backbone and ITIS TSN 180172.

common_names.note: en/fr/es labels; the English name is the primary one, 'Eastern fox squirrel' being the alternative given in the Wikipedia lead, and the fr/es labels are the Wikidata sitelink titles.

range.note: Native list from 'its natural range extends through most of the eastern United States, north into the southern prairie provinces of Canada, west to the Dakotas, Colorado, and Texas, and south to the northern parts of Coahuila, Nuevo Leon ... and Tamaulipas'. Introduced list from 'It has been introduced to both northern and southern California, Oregon, Idaho, Montana, Washington, New Mexico, and Utah, as well as Ontario and British Columbia in Canada'. Koppen classes are the author's judgement of the described range.

traits.body_plan.note: Vertebrate, chordate, four-legged, furred, endothermic mammal.

traits.limb_count.note: Quadruped: four legs, as a rodent.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: 'Fox squirrels are strictly diurnal, non-territorial, and spend more of their time on the ground than most other tree squirrels. They are still, however, agile climbers', so a ground walk and a climb are the two gaits; the block model has no climb pose, so walking carries the locomotion.

traits.thermoregulation.note: Endotherm: a mammal, active in daylight and denning overnight.

traits.skin.note: Fur: 'the upper body is brown-grey to brown-yellow with a typically brownish-orange underside' in the usual morph, with dark brown and black patterned and all-black morphs in parts of the range.

traits.flight.note: None: a ground-and-tree rodent that does not glide or fly.

traits.metamorphosis.note: None: 'At birth, the young are blind, without fur, and helpless', with eyes opening at 4-5 weeks.

traits.nest_type.note: A tree cavity (den) preferred over a leaf nest for winter and for raising young, with a leaf nest (drey) used when den trees are scarce.

traits.perching.note: False, following the existing sciurus-carolinensis record: the fox squirrel climbs and sits in the canopy to nest, using tree forks, hollows and platforms about 9 m up, but the schema's perching flag describes a bird perching on a branch, and no passerine perch pose exists for a quadruped mesh. The climb itself is carried in traits.locomotion_modes.

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg (0.794 kg, in the Small band under 1 kg). shoulder_height_m is deliberately omitted: the article gives total length, body length and hind-foot length (5.1-8.2 cm) but no standing height, and converting a hind-foot measurement into one would be an invention. The validator's MissingShoulderHeight warning is accepted for that reason, as it is in the existing sciurus-carolinensis record.

traits.mass_kg.note: Midpoint of 'They range in weight from 1.0 to 2.5 lb (453.6 to 1,134.0 g)'.

traits.mass_range_kg.note: 'They range in weight from 1.0 to 2.5 lb (453.6 to 1,134.0 g).'

traits.length_m.note: Midpoint of 'total length measures 20 to 30 in (50.8 to 76.2 cm)'. (The body alone is 25.4-38.1 cm with a similar tail length; the schema's length_m takes the animal's total length.)

traits.lifespan_y.note: The article gives no mean lifespan, only 'The reproductive longevity of the squirrel may be over 12 years' and that females are 'sexually mature at 10 to 11 months of age'. lifespan_y is therefore authored at 12 as an upper bound taken from the stated reproductive longevity, not a sourced mean lifespan.

traits.diet.note: Shares follow the article's own ranking of mast as the staple ('rely heavily on hickories from late August through September', 'prefer hickory nuts, acorns, corn, and black walnuts', 'Autumn foods consist mainly of acorns, hickory nuts, beechnuts, walnuts, butternuts, and hazelnuts') with the spring bud-and-insect diet, the summer berry and fruit diet, and the occasional bird eggs taken from the Michigan list. The percentages themselves are the author's judgement, as the article ranks the foods without quantifying them.

traits.social.note: 'Fox squirrels are strictly diurnal, non-territorial'; the article's social unit is the pair sharing a den ('Cohabitation of these dens is not uncommon, particularly among breeding pairs') and the family denning together, so structure Group with a small range is used, with solo foraging the norm.

traits.defense.note: Authored: the article lists a long set of predators (bobcat, fox, raptors, owls, coyote) and says 'Relatively few natural predators can regularly capture adult fox squirrels', with no defensive display of its own, so Flee is the closest schema value.

traits.wariness.note: 'Fox squirrels are tolerant of human proximity, and even thrive in crowded urban and suburban environments. They exploit human habitations for sources of food and nesting sites.'

habitat.use.note: The article says it spends more time on the ground than other tree squirrels, is 'often observed foraging on the ground several hundred meters from the nearest woodlot', nests in tree cavities and forks about 9 m up, and climbs to reach mast. Ground and arboreal use are therefore balanced, unlike the more arboreal gray squirrel.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: 'Fox squirrels have two types of shelters: leaf nests (dreys) and tree dens ... Tree dens are preferred over leaf nests during the winter and for raising young', and existing cavities are the usual site.

habitat.resources.note: The mast, seed, fruit, browse and invertebrate weights follow the diet shares, with small_vertebrate for the bird eggs in the Michigan list; cavity is the nesting and wintering shelter and perch the canopy rest.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: urban_affinity and uses_gardens from 'They exploit human habitations for sources of food and nesting sites, being as happy nesting in an attic as they are in a hollow tree' and from 'most often found in forest patches of 40 hectares or less with an open understory, or in urban neighborhoods with trees'; light_max, flight_distance_m and road_mortality are judgement values, the article giving no figures.

seasonal.strategy.note: Resident: 'Fox squirrels are strictly diurnal, non-territorial' with no mention of migration, and the article describes year-round foraging on stored caches.

seasonal.phases.note: The biology is stated without calendar months: 'come into estrus in mid-December or early January, then again in June', 'Gestation occurs over a period of 44 to 45 days', 'The earliest litters appear in late January; most births occur in mid-March and July', and caches are formed in autumn. Every phase boundary is the author's judgement, placed by counting the stated gestation back from the stated birth months.

seasonal.life_stages.note: 'Fox squirrels are weaned between 12 and 14 weeks, but may not be self-supporting until 16 weeks. Juveniles usually disperse in September or October'. duration_days is the 16-week age at which a juvenile is self-supporting, and scale is a judgement of a young animal at weaning.

look.note: Pelage from the Description section: 'In most areas, the animal's upper body is brown-grey to brown-yellow with a typically brownish-orange underside', with darker patterned and all-black morphs in parts of the range; the record draws the common eastern morph. Proportions are judgement, scaled for a heavy-bodied, bushy-tailed tree squirrel, and the tail_fluff part thickens the tail to the bushy outline the description gives.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared ground-forager program, which is the only ground-mammal program available: mast-led foraging, a short flee distance for an animal that habituates to people, and the daytime rest window (-90 to -6 degrees) the program documents for a diurnal species, since the fox squirrel is strictly diurnal.
